CASE REPORTS

cases.text:
Patient 1. This patient, a 50-year-old African-
American woman, presented with a I-year history of pro-
gressive stiffness of her lower extremities and difficulty
walking. Previously, there had been transient improvement
with a combination of physical therapy and diazepam.
Several months earlier, treatment with prednisone, 60 mg/
day, and a course of 5 plasmapheresis treatments had
resulted in a gain of 15" of flexion in both hips and the right
knee. However, at the time of admission, she had persistent
extensor tone of both lower extremities, with virtually no
flexion of the hips, and she could not walk. There was
hyperextension and spasm of both knees, and the ankles
were maintained in constant plantar flexion. She was begun
on a regimen of diazepam 5 mg 4 times a day and baclofen 20
mg 3 times a day.
The electromyogram (EMG) showed continuous mo-
tor unit activity in the lower extremities and normal findings
in the upper extremities. Serum anti-GAD antibodies were
detected by immunocytochemical assay. Treatment with
diazepam, baclofen, carbamazepine, and valproic acid did
not result in any improvement, nor did an intrathecal infu-
sion of baclofen.
Because of her lack of progress, treatment with IVIG
was initiated, at a dosage of 400 mgkg/day for 5 consecutive
days. Improvement in bilateral hip and right knee flexion
was noted within a few days; IVIG therapy was repeated
(400 mglkglday for 3 infusions) on a monthly basis. Follow-
ing her third month of WIG therapy, hip flexion increased to
70" bilaterally, right knee flexion to 90", and left knee flexion
to 10". She was able to walk with the use of a walker. The
prednisone was gradually discontinued, and daily doses of
baclofen and diazepam were reduced.

Patient 2. This patient, a 43-year-old African-
American woman, presented with a 3-year history of pro-
gressive muscle stiffness, with spasms of the legs and lower
back. On 3 occasions over a 3-year period, she had been

admitted to the psychiatry service of a community hospital
for episodes of muscle rigidity that had been diagnosed as
hysterical conversion reactions; she had been treated with
diazepam. Physical examination revealed a hyperlordotic
posture, with severe paraspinous muscle spasm and rigid
abdominal and lower extremity muscles. The hips, knees,
and ankles could not be flexed. Results of magnetic reso-
nance imaging (MRI) of the thoracolumbar spine were nor-
mal. An EMG of the lower extremities revealed continuous
motor-unit activity. Serum anti-GAD autobodies were posi-
tive by immunocytochemical assay. Anti-islet cell antibod-
ies were positive at a titer of 1:15,360.
The patient was treated with clonazepam 2 mg twice
a day, prednisone 80 mglday, and 5 plasmapheresis treat-
ments. There was sustained improvement over the next
year, but her condition relapsed when the prednisone was
stopped. She became bedridden and was admitted to the
hospital.
Soh-Medrol (Upjohn, Kalamazoo, MI), 1 gm intra-
venously, was administered daily for 3 days, along with 12
mg of clonazepam daily, but there was no benefit. An
additional daily dose of 60 mg prednisone for 4 days did not
result in any improvement. WIG (400 mg/kg/day) was given
for 5 consecutive days. Following the second dose, the
patient noted a dramatic reduction in her painful muscle
spasms and less stiffness. Flexibility continued to improve
throughout the IVIG therapy. When the patient was dis-
charged she was able to flex her knees to 90" and to walk
with the aid of a walker.
A second cycle of IVIG was administered 6 weeks
later, when her stiffness began to return. Clinical improve-
ment was noted during the intravenous infusion cycle, and
she remained ambulatory. A third cycle of IVIG adminis-
tered 5 months later was associated with an improvement in
the patient's gait and mobility.

Patient 3. This patient, a 69-year-old Caucasian
woman, was seen because of her recent inability to walk. Six
years earlier, a diagnosis of epilepsy had been established.
Her seizures were focal and characterized by speech distur-
bance and rigidity of the right lower extremity. She was
maintained on a regimen of sodium valproate and diazepam.
Four months prior to admission, she noted the onset of left
lower extremity stiffness and difficulty walking.
Physical examination revealed an extended left knee
to 180" and extreme plantar flexion of the left ankle and foot.
The patient could not walk. Results of MRI of the head and
lumbar spine were unremarkable. An EMG of the lower
extremities revealed continuous motor-unit activity. Anti-
GAD antibodies were negative by immunocytochemical
assay.
The diazepam dosage was increased to 15 mg/day,
with some clinical improvement noted; however, she be-
came confused and disoriented as a result of this treatment.
IVIG was begun (400 mg/kg/day for 5 days) and following the
second infusion, the patient noted a marked resolution of left
leg stiffness. She regained independent mobility for the next
5 weeks. Over the next 3 months, 2 additional courses of
WIG therapy were administered after the patient became
stiff and unable to walk. Each course resulted in a rapid
return to full, independent ambulation.
METHODS
Immunocytochemistry. Immunorhodamine and
immunoperoxidase staining of frozen tissue sections and
primary cell cultures was carried out as previously described
(2,3). Rat tissues were fixed by transcardiac perfusion. Small
fragments of apparently normal human cerebral cortex were
fixed by immersion. Patients' sera were used at dilutions of
1:20 to 1 :30 for immunofluorescence and at 1: 150 for immuno-
peroxidase.
DISCUSSION
All 3 patients exhibited clinical and laboratory
features of SMS (Table 2). The presence of intense
muscle rigidity in the back and lower extremities with
rock-hard, board-like muscles is characteristic. Electro-
myographic evidence of continuous motor-unit activ-
ity, without other abnormalities, is also typical of SMS

(1). Solimena et a1 (2,3) have identified anti-GAD
antibodies in the majority of patients. Recently, those
authors described autoantibodies to a 128-kd synaptic
protein in 3 women with SMS and breast cancer who
did not have anti-GAD antibodies (6). Grimaldi et a1 (7)
have defined 3 diagnostic subsets of patients. The first
group have autoimmune features, including insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease, as
well as the presence of multiple autoantibodies, such
as anti-GAD, anti-islet cell, and other organic-specific
antibodies.
The second group of patients are anti-GAD
antibody negative but have autoantibodies to other
synaptic proteins, without the presence of organ-
specific autoantibodies. These patients have devel-
oped malignancies, including breast carcinoma, colon
carcinoma, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma. The third group
of SMS patients do not display any autoimmune
features clinically and are anti-GAD antibody nega-
tive. Patients 1 and 2 belong to the first group, and
patient 3 to the third group.
While SMS is considered to be an autoimmune
disorder, the pathophysiology is poorly understood.
There is a dominant autoimmune response directed
against GAD in a high proportion of patients, with
intrathecal production of the autoantibody (2,3). GAD
is an intracellular enzyme involved in the synthesis of
the neurotransmitter GABA in the central nervous
system. GAD is specifically present within GABA
neurons, but is not expressed as a cell surface antigen.
The rigidity and spasm seen clinically reflect a prepon-
derance of excitatory over inhibitory influences on the
motor neuron pool. A deficiency of GABA-mediated
inhibition at the spinal and/or supraspinal level has
been proposed (3). Solimena et al(2) found that serum
from affected patients reacts with nerve terminals of
cerebellar basket cells in the rat. In human SMS, it is
unclear whether symptoms are a direct result of dam-
age to GABA-synthetic enzymes or some other neu-
ronal target. The rapid response to IVIG in our 3
patients suggests that the autoantibodies might have
some direct action on GABA release or a blocking
effect at an ion exchange channel or synaptic receptor.
Intravenous immune globulin has been used in
the treatment of such neurologic autoimmune diseases
as myasthenia gravis (8,9), multiple sclerosis (lo),
Guillain-Barre syndrome (1 l), demyelinating poly-
neuropathy (12), and polymyositis (13). Given the
refractory nature of our patients’ clinical conditions,
we elected to treat with IVIG. The striking and rapid
onset of clinical improvement in our 3 patients may
suggest that IVIG is effective via an antiidiotypic
antibody mechanism. Antiidiotypic antibodies capable
of binding to the idiotypic region of a specific disease-
associated autoantibody can be found in IVIG and in
the serum of patients recovering from a disease asso-
ciated with that autoantibody, but they cannot be
found in the serum of healthy subjects (14). Alterna-
tively, receptors for the Fc portion of IgG on reticu-
loendothelial cells may be blocked by IVIG impairing
their ability to function (8).
The neurologic improvement in our patients
following peripheral administration of IVIG suggests
that immune globulin administered intravenously af-
fects the production and action of autoantibodies in
the intrathecal compartment and central nervous sys-
tem. In theory, the blood-brain barrier excludes exog-
enously administered IgG, though Sekul et a1 (15)
demonstrated that IgG is elevated in the cerebrospinal
fluid following peripheral intravenous administration.
Due to the nature of the immunocytochemical assay
used, we could not quantify a change in the titer of
the anti-GAD antibodies before and after treatment
with IVIG.
The natural course of SMS is one of steady,
slow progression of the disease (16). Spontaneous
remissions are extremely unusual and would be an
unlikely explanation for our patients’ clinical improve-
ment. Although a delayed benefit from corticosteroid
therapy may occur, both corticosteroid-treated pa-
tients had been receiving at least 60 mg prednisone per
day for several weeks without benefit prior to treat-
ment with IVIG. Prior to initiation of treatment with
IVIG, all 3 patients were treated with maximally
tolerated doses of diazepam but remained bedridden.
Following IVIG therapy the doses of concomitant
drugs, including corticosteroids, diazepam, and ba-
clofen, could be reduced in all 3 patients.
We suggest that further studies are essential to
verify our initial observations of clinical benefit with
the use of IVIG in SMS.
